awd_titl_txt: Collaborative Research: MFB: Integrating Deep Learning and High-throughput Experimentation to Rapidly Navigate Protein Fitness Landscapes for Non-native Enzyme Catalysis
awd_abstract_narration:
Understanding the relationship between protein structure and function remains a major challenge. This knowledge would benefit drug design, recycling, and chemical production. This project is designed to learn how to create proteins that will facilitate reactions seen in nature. Artificial intelligence will interpret the data generated by experiments. Two classes of enzymes will be modified to facilitate novel reactions. To help diversify the STEM workforce, workshops in machine learning will be offered to students interested in protein design. Summer research opportunities will be offered to high school and undergraduate students traditionally underrepresented in STEM fields.

In this project, protein engineering is treated as a Bayesian optimization problem, with the objective to explore sequence space for improved specific activity. This approach models both the expected activity and the uncertainty of the prediction made. Training deep learning models is data intensive. A convolution neural net (CNN) using transformer architecture will use simulated sequence-function data to pretrain.  The simulated data will be generated using Rosetta. Pretrained CNN will be refined with experimental data generated using combinatorial codon mutagenesis (CCM).  Enzyme activity in single bacterial cells will be monitored using GFP expression, FACS-based screening, and next-generation DNA sequencing to determine the corresponding amino acid sequences.  Biosensor screening can suffer from crosstalk when multiple cells are present. A picoliter-scale microdroplet screening technology developed in the Romero lab will be utilized to avoid this issue.  A simulated annealing algorithm to randomly search over sequence positions and degenerate codons for libraries with high values for the expected batch BO objective will be developed. In addition, a probabilistic program using sampling-based inference to estimate the optimal combination of codons will be designed and implemented.

This project is jointly supported by the Division of Chemical, Bioengineering, Environmental and Transport Systems (CBET), the Division of Chemistry (CHE), and the Division of Information and Intelligent Systems (IIS).

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Proteins are tiny molecular machines that make living things work. They can also be engineered to perform useful tasks, such as making medicines and chemicals, breaking down waste, or carrying out chemical reactions that are difficult to accomplish using traditional methods. The challenge is that proteins are extraordinarily complex, and we still do not understand the rules needed to design them and fully harness their potential.

This project explored how artificial intelligence and new experimental technologies can work together to make protein engineering faster and more systematic. Researchers in computer science, engineering, and chemistry worked together to develop methods in which computer models learn from experimental results and then help determine which proteins should be tested next.

One major outcome was a new approach called METL that allows artificial intelligence models to learn from computer simulations of proteins before being trained on experimental measurements. These simulations provide the model with basic information about how protein molecules behave. As a result, the model can learn effectively from much smaller amounts of experimental data. We showed experimentally that this approach could be used to design new functional proteins even when relatively few proteins had previously been tested. This work was published in Nature Methods.


The project also addressed the experimental side of this problem. We developed a technology called OMEGA that makes it possible to build large collections of precisely specified genes in parallel. This provides a way to physically create and test the many protein designs generated by computational methods. The work was published in Science Advances.
Finally, we used artificial intelligence to learn from experimental data and design improved enzymes. We trained AI models on measurements collected from hundreds of enzyme variants, allowing the models to learn how changes in an enzyme’s sequence affect its activity. We then used these models to predict new enzyme designs that were expected to perform better. When we built and tested the predicted enzymes in the laboratory, most showed improved activity, with the best designs improving activity approximately three-fold. Importantly, the AI identified beneficial changes that had not been discovered through the original experimental search. This work demonstrates how AI can learn from experimental results, identify useful patterns that are difficult to recognize otherwise, and use that knowledge to design better enzymes.

The project also provided interdisciplinary training for young scientists working across artificial intelligence, biology, and chemistry. Researchers gained experience in both computational and experimental science, presented their work at scientific meetings, and participated in public outreach activities explaining enzymes and biotechnology. Overall, this project developed new ways for AI and experiments to work together to make protein engineering faster and more efficient.
